title: Salutations et au revoir / Greetings and Farewells
bridge: Greetings in French are very ritualized: it is important to know when to use 'bonjour' (formal, during the day), 'bonsoir' (from the evening onwards) and 'salut' (informal among friends). A cultural trap: in France, it is very rude to enter a shop or address someone without greeting them first. Always say 'bonjour, monsieur/madame' before anything else. 'Ça va?' is a greeting formula, not a genuine question about your health.
rule: Formal greetings: Bonjour (good morning/good afternoon), Bonsoir (good evening, arrival), Bonne nuit (good night, farewell for sleeping). Informal greetings: Salut! (hi), Coucou! (very informal, among friends). Formal farewells: Au revoir (goodbye), Bonne journée (have a good day), Bonsoir (good evening upon arrival). Informal: Salut! À bientôt! (see you soon), À plus! (colloquial abbreviation), À tout à l'heure (see you later, if they will meet soon).

concept_examples.translation: Good morning, ma'am. How are you?
Hi! How's it going?
Goodbye and have a nice day!
See you soon!

common_error.wrong: Bonne nuit! (al entrar a un bar por la noche)
common_error.explanation: 'Bonne nuit' is only said when someone is going to SLEEP (good night for resting). To greet someone at night when arriving somewhere, you say 'Bonsoir'. The equivalent of 'good evening' upon arrival is 'Bonsoir'.

examples.original: Bonjour, monsieur. Comment allez-vous?
examples.translation: Good morning, sir. How are you?
examples.note: 'Comment allez-vous?' is the formal form. Response: 'Très bien, merci. Et vous?'

examples.original: Bonsoir, madame Dupont.
examples.translation: Good evening, Mrs. Dupont.
examples.note: 'Bonsoir' is used from approximately 5-6 PM onwards.

examples.original: Au revoir, à demain.
examples.translation: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.
examples.note: 'À demain' = see you tomorrow. Useful when saying goodbye to coworkers.

examples.original: Salut! Ça va?
examples.translation: Hi! How's it going?
examples.note: 'Ça va?' is informal. Responses: 'Ça va bien!', 'Pas mal', 'Bof...' (so-so).

examples.original: Coucou! T'es là?
examples.translation: Hey! Are you there?
examples.note: 'Coucou' is very colloquial, among close friends or playfully.

examples.original: À plus! À tout à l'heure!
examples.translation: See you later! See you in a bit!
examples.note: 'À plus' (colloquial) = see you later. 'À tout à l'heure' = see you very soon (if they will meet soon).

examples.original: Bonne journée, monsieur!
examples.translation: Have a good day, sir!
examples.note: Very common in shops, offices. Response: 'Merci, vous aussi!'

examples.original: Bon week-end!
examples.translation: Have a good weekend!
examples.note: When saying goodbye on Friday. Response: 'Merci, bon week-end à vous aussi!'

examples.original: Bonne nuit, dors bien!
examples.translation: Good night, sleep well!
examples.note: 'Bonne nuit' only when someone is going to sleep.

title: Se présenter / Introducing yourself and others
bridge: Introducing yourself in French is similar to Spanish but with some specific formulas. The main difference: in French you don't say 'me llamo' with a direct reflexive as in Spanish. You use 'je m'appelle' (literally 'I call myself') or 'je suis' (I am). For professions, in French NO article is used: 'je suis professeur' (not 'je suis UN professeur'). This is different from Spanish where an article is used in some contexts.
rule: Introducing yourself: Je m'appelle + name, Je suis + name/profession, J'ai + age + ans, J'habite à + city, Je viens de + city/country, Je parle + language. To introduce others: Voici mon ami(e) + name (here is my friend), Je vous présente + name (I introduce to you..., formal), C'est + name (this is..., informal). To ask for a name: Comment tu t'appelles? (informal) / Comment vous appelez-vous? (formal).

concept_examples.text: Je m'appelle Sophie et j'ai vingt-cinq ans.
concept_examples.translation: My name is Sophie and I am twenty-five years old.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə mapɛl sɔfi e ʒe vɛ̃t sɛ̃k‿ɑ̃/

concept_examples.text: Je suis espagnol et j'habite à Barcelone.
concept_examples.translation: I am Spanish and I live in Barcelona.

concept_examples.text: Je vous présente ma collègue, Amélie.
concept_examples.translation: I introduce to you my colleague, Amélie.
I am a law student.

common_error.explanation: With professions after 'être', in French NO article is used: 'je suis médecin', 'elle est avocate', 'il est ingénieur'. However, when specifying more: 'C'est un bon médecin' (it does take an article).

examples.original: Bonjour, je m'appelle Carlos. Et toi?
examples.translation: Hello, my name is Carlos. And you?
examples.note: 'Et toi?' = And you? Very common to return the question.

examples.original: J'ai trente ans et je viens d'Espagne.
examples.translation: I am thirty years old and I come from Spain.
examples.note: 'Je viens de' for origin. With a city: je viens de Madrid.

examples.original: J'habite à Paris depuis deux ans.
examples.translation: I live in Paris for two years.
examples.note: 'Depuis' = for/since. Very useful to give context.

levels.label: Présenter sa profession et ses langues

examples.original: Je suis médecin et je travaille à Lyon.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə sɥi medsɛ̃ e ʒə tʁavaj a ljɔ̃/
examples.translation: I am a doctor and I work in Lyon.
examples.note: Profession without article after 'être'.

examples.original: Je parle espagnol, français et un peu d'anglais.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə paʁl ɛspaɲɔl fʁɑ̃sɛ e œ̃ pø dɑ̃ɡlɛ/
examples.translation: I speak Spanish, French, and a little English.
examples.note: 'Un peu de' = a little. Languages without article after 'parler'.

examples.original: J'étudie le français depuis six mois.
examples.translation: I have been studying French for six months.
examples.note: 'Depuis' + time. Here 'le français' takes an article because it is a direct object.

examples.original: Je te présente mon ami Thomas.
examples.translation: I introduce to you my friend Thomas.
examples.note: 'Je te présente' (informal), 'je vous présente' (formal/plural).

examples.original: C'est ma femme, Elena. Elle est espagnole.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ ma fam elena ɛl ɛ ɛspaɲɔl/
examples.translation: This is my wife, Elena. She is Spanish.
examples.note: 'C'est' for informal introduction. Nationality: adjective agrees.

examples.original: Voici mon collègue, Monsieur Renaud.
examples.translation: Here is my colleague, Mr. Renaud.
examples.note: 'Voici' = here is. Formal for introducing in a professional context.

title: Origine et nationalité / Origin and nationality
bridge: Talking about origin in French is quite straightforward. The key difference from Spanish: nationalities have gender in French (like in Spanish) but country names have definite articles that sometimes disappear with prepositions. Additionally, nationality names are written in LOWERCASE when they are adjectives: 'je suis espagnol', but in UPPERCASE when they are nouns: 'un Espagnol'. This distinction does not exist in Spanish.
rule: Asking origin: D'où viens-tu? / Tu viens d'où? (informal) / Vous venez d'où? / De quelle nationalité êtes-vous? (formal). Responding: Je viens de + city/country (with the appropriate preposition). Je suis + nationality (in lowercase as an adjective). Common nationalities: français(e), espagnol(e), anglais(e), allemand(e), italien(ne), américain(e), argentin(e), mexicain(e), chinois(e), japonais(e). Countries: la France, l'Espagne, l'Angleterre, l'Allemagne, l'Italie, les États-Unis.

concept_examples.text: Je suis espagnole, je viens de Séville.
concept_examples.translation: I am Spanish, I come from Seville.
What nationality are you?

concept_examples.text: Il est américain mais il habite en France.
concept_examples.translation: He is American but he lives in France.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛ nameʁikɛ̃ mɛ il abit ɑ̃ fʁɑ̃s/

concept_examples.translation: Where do you come from?

common_error.explanation: In French, nationalities in lowercase are adjectives: 'je suis espagnol/française/américaine'. In uppercase they are nouns: 'un Espagnol' (a Spanish man), 'une Française' (a French woman). Different from Spanish where it is always written with a capital letter in some contexts.

examples.original: D'où tu viens? - Je viens d'Espagne.
examples.translation: Where do you come from? - I come from Spain.
examples.note: 'De + feminine country': de France, d'Espagne, d'Italie (elides before a vowel).

examples.original: Je viens du Mexique.
examples.translation: I come from Mexico.
examples.note: 'Du' (de + le) with masculine countries: du Mexique, du Maroc, du Japon.

examples.original: Elle vient des États-Unis.
examples.translation: She comes from the United States.
examples.note: 'Des' (de + les) with plural countries.

examples.original: Je suis espagnol / espagnole.
examples.translation: I am Spanish (male/female).
examples.note: The feminine form adds -e: espagnol → espagnole (pronounce the l).

examples.original: Il est français, elle est française.
examples.translation: He is French, she is French.
examples.note: français → française: the cedilla disappears and the final -se is pronounced /z/.

examples.original: Ils sont mexicains, elles sont mexicaines.
examples.translation: They are Mexican (males), they are Mexican (females).
examples.note: Plural: mexicains/mexicaines. Gender distinction in plural.

levels.label: Conversations sur l'origine et les langues

examples.original: Tu parles bien français pour quelqu'un d'espagnol!
examples.phonetic: /ty paʁl bjɛ̃ fʁɑ̃sɛ puʁ kɛlkœ̃ dɛspaɲɔl/
examples.translation: You speak French well for a Spanish person!
examples.note: 'Pour quelqu'un de + nationality' = for being + nationality.

examples.original: Je suis à moitié italien, à moitié argentin.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə sɥiz‿a mwatje italijɛ̃ a mwatje aʁʒɑ̃tɛ̃/
examples.translation: I am half Italian, half Argentine.
examples.note: 'À moitié' = half, halfway.

examples.original: Dans ma famille, on parle trois langues.
examples.phonetic: /dɑ̃ ma famij ɔ̃ paʁl tʁwa lɑ̃ɡ/
examples.translation: In my family, we speak three languages.
examples.note: 'On parle' = one speaks/we speak. Use of 'on' as 'we'.

title: Décrire des personnes et des objets / Describing people and objects
bridge: Describing in French requires remembering gender and number agreement in adjectives, and that most adjectives go AFTER the noun. To describe physical appearance, the verbs 'être' (to be) and 'avoir' (to have) are used: 'il est grand' but 'il a les cheveux noirs' (he has black hair). This combination of being with having for description is different from Spanish, where everything usually goes with 'ser'.
rule: To describe people: être + adjective of size/character/general appearance (il est grand, elle est sympa). Avoir + les cheveux/les yeux + adjective for specific features (il a les cheveux blonds, elle a les yeux verts). To describe objects: C'est + un/une + adjective + noun (c'est un grand livre) or the noun + adjective (c'est un livre intéressant). Very useful: quel/quelle (what + noun): Quelle belle maison!

concept_examples.text: Il est grand et mince avec les cheveux noirs.
concept_examples.translation: He is tall and slim with black hair.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il ɛ ɡʁɑ̃ e mɛ̃s avɛk le ʃəvø nwaʁ/

concept_examples.text: C'est un sac rouge et très pratique.
concept_examples.translation: It's a red and very practical bag.
concept_examples.phonetic: /sɛ tœ̃ sak ʁuʒ e tʁɛ pʁatik/

concept_examples.text: Elle a l'air sympa et intelligente.
concept_examples.translation: She seems nice and intelligent.
What is your new car like?

common_error.explanation: To describe physical features with 'avoir', always use the definite article: 'il a LES cheveux blonds, LES yeux bleus'. The adjective goes after the noun. Never 'avoir + adj + noun'.

examples.original: Mon frère est grand et mince.
examples.translation: My brother is tall and slim.
examples.note: grand/grande (tall), petit/petite (short), mince (slim), gros/grosse (fat).

examples.original: Elle a les cheveux longs et les yeux bleus.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl a le ʃəvø lɔ̃ e lez‿jø blø/
examples.translation: She has long hair and blue eyes.
examples.note: 'Avoir les cheveux + adj'. Colors go after: cheveux noirs, roux, bruns, blonds.

examples.original: Il a l'air fatigué aujourd'hui.
examples.translation: He looks tired today.
examples.note: 'Avoir l'air + adj' = to seem. Very useful for describing apparent states.

examples.original: Ma professeure est très sympa et patiente.
examples.phonetic: /ma pʁɔfɛsœʁ ɛ tʁɛ sɛ̃pa e pasjɑ̃t/
examples.translation: My teacher is very nice and patient.
examples.note: sympa (nice, invariable), gentil/gentille (kind), sérieux/sérieuse (serious).

examples.original: Il est un peu timide mais très intelligent.
examples.phonetic: /il ɛ œ̃ pø timid mɛ tʁɛz‿ɛ̃tɛliʒɑ̃/
examples.translation: He is a little shy but very intelligent.
examples.note: 'Un peu' = a little. 'Mais' = but.

examples.original: Elle est drôle et toujours de bonne humeur.
examples.phonetic: /ɛl ɛ dʁol e tuʒuʁ də bɔn ymœʁ/
examples.translation: She is funny and always in a good mood.
examples.note: 'Être de bonne humeur' = to be in a good mood.

examples.original: C'est un petit appartement mais très lumineux.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ tœ̃ pəti tapaʁtəmɑ̃ mɛ tʁɛ lyminø/
examples.translation: It's a small apartment but very bright.
examples.note: 'Petit' goes before the noun; 'lumineux' after.

examples.original: Ce téléphone est vieux et lent.
examples.translation: This phone is old and slow.
examples.note: Description of objects: être + adjective(s) separated by 'et'.

examples.original: Quelle belle vue! C'est magnifique.
examples.translation: What a beautiful view! It's magnificent.
examples.note: 'Quelle + adj + nom' for exclamations. 'Quel/quelle/quels/quelles' according to gender and number.

title: Goûts et préférences / Expressing likes and dislikes
bridge: In Spanish we say 'me gusta' with the verb gustar which works in reverse. In French, likes are expressed more directly: 'j'aime' (I love/I like very much), 'j'aime bien' (I like), 'j'adore' (I love/adore) and 'je n'aime pas' (I don't like). A trap: in French 'j'aime' is stronger than in Spanish; among friends you can say 'j'aime bien' for ordinary 'me gusta'. 'J'aime' alone can sound like romantic love in certain contexts.
rule: Scale of likes in French (from most to least): j'adore (I love), j'aime beaucoup (I like very much), j'aime (I like/I love), j'aime bien (I like), ça m'est égal (it's all the same to me), je n'aime pas trop (I don't like very much), je n'aime pas (I don't like), je déteste (I hate), j'ai horreur de (I'm horrified by). Structure: aimer/adorer/détester + infinitive or + noun (with article).

concept_examples.text: J'adore le chocolat mais je n'aime pas le café.
concept_examples.translation: I love chocolate but I don't like coffee.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒadɔʁ lə ʃɔkɔla mɛ ʒə nɛm pa lə kafe/

concept_examples.translation: Do you like music?

concept_examples.text: Je préfère le cinéma à la télévision.
concept_examples.translation: I prefer cinema to television.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə pʁefɛʁ lə sinema a la televizjɔ̃/

concept_examples.translation: I'm horrified by spiders!

common_error.explanation: After 'aimer/adorer' in affirmative, the definite article is used: j'aime LE chocolat, j'adore LA musique. In negative: je n'aime pas LE sport (the article is kept). 'du/de la' is not used here.

examples.original: J'aime beaucoup le cinéma français.
examples.translation: I really like French cinema.
examples.note: 'Beaucoup' after the verb reinforces the liking.

examples.original: Elle adore voyager.
examples.translation: She loves to travel.
examples.note: With infinitive directly: adorer + infinitive.

examples.original: Je déteste faire la vaisselle.
examples.translation: I hate doing the dishes.
examples.note: 'Détester' = to hate. 'Faire la vaisselle' = to do the dishes.

examples.original: Je préfère le thé au café.
examples.translation: I prefer tea to coffee.
examples.note: 'Préférer A à B' = to prefer A over B. Note the form 'au' (à + le).

examples.original: Ça m'est égal, je mange tout.
examples.translation: It's all the same to me, I eat everything.
examples.note: 'Ça m'est égal' = it's all the same to me, I don't care.

examples.original: J'aime bien la montagne mais je préfère la mer.
examples.phonetic: /ʒɛm bjɛ̃ la mɔ̃taɲ mɛ ʒə pʁefɛʁ la mɛʁ/
examples.translation: I like the mountains but I prefer the sea.
examples.note: 'J'aime bien' (I like) vs 'j'aime' (I like/I love).

levels.label: Parler de ses loisirs et intérêts

examples.original: Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire le week-end?
examples.phonetic: /kɛs kə ty ɛm fɛʁ lə wikɛnd/
examples.translation: What do you like to do on the weekend?
examples.note: 'Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire?' = what do you like to do? Very common question.

examples.original: Je suis passionné(e) de musique classique.
examples.translation: I am passionate about classical music.
examples.note: 'Être passionné(e) de' = to be passionate about, stronger than 'aimer'.

examples.original: En ce moment, j'ai un faible pour la cuisine thaïe.
examples.phonetic: /ɑ̃ sə mɔmɑ̃ ʒe œ̃ fɛbl puʁ la kɥizin tai/
examples.translation: Right now, I have a weakness for Thai cuisine.
examples.note: 'Avoir un faible pour' = to have a weakness for. More sophisticated expression.

title: Commander au restaurant / Ordering food and drink in a restaurant
bridge: Ordering in a French restaurant has important rituals. First: you never interrupt a waiter; you wait to make eye contact. Second: you order using the conditional 'je voudrais' (I would like) instead of the present 'je veux' (I want), which can sound abrupt. The menu in France has a special meaning: 'le menu' is the fixed-price menu (starter+main+dessert), while 'la carte' is the à la carte menu with all individual dishes.
rule: Ordering politely: Je voudrais + noun (I would like...), Je prends + noun (I'll have...), Pour moi, + noun (For me...). Calling the waiter: Excusez-moi, monsieur/madame! The waiter may say: Vous avez choisi? (Have you chosen?), Qu'est-ce que vous prenez? (What will you have?), Et comme boisson? (And to drink?), C'est pour emporter? (Is it to take away?). Asking for the bill: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.

concept_examples.text: Je voudrais un steak-frites, s'il vous plaît.
concept_examples.translation: I would like a steak with fries, please.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə vudʁɛ œ̃ stɛk fʁit sil vu plɛ/

concept_examples.translation: For me, the Niçoise salad.
The bill, please.

concept_examples.text: Est-ce que vous avez une table pour deux?
concept_examples.translation: Do you have a table for two?
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛs kə vuz‿ave yn tabl puʁ dø/

common_error.wrong: Je veux le poulet rôti. (brusco en restaurante)
common_error.correct: Je voudrais le poulet rôti, s'il vous plaît.
common_error.correct_alt: Je vais prendre le poulet rôti.
common_error.explanation: In a French restaurant, 'je veux' (I want) sounds direct and even rude. It is always preferable to use 'je voudrais' (I would like) or 'je vais prendre' (I will have). This difference in register is very important in French culture.

levels.label: Réserver et demander une table
levels.translation: Reserving and asking for a table

examples.original: Bonjour, j'ai une réservation au nom de Garcia.
examples.phonetic: /bɔ̃ʒuʁ ʒe yn ʁezɛʁvasjɔ̃ o nɔ̃ də ɡaʁsja/
examples.translation: Hello, I have a reservation under the name Garcia.
examples.note: 'Au nom de' = under the name of. Formula to identify the reservation.

examples.original: Une table pour trois personnes, s'il vous plaît.
examples.phonetic: /yn tabl puʁ tʁwa pɛʁsɔn sil vu plɛ/
examples.translation: A table for three people, please.
examples.note: Specify the number of people when asking for a table.

examples.original: Est-ce qu'on peut avoir une table en terrasse?
examples.phonetic: /ɛs kɔ̃ pø avwaʁ yn tabl ɑ̃ tɛʁas/
examples.translation: Can we have a table on the terrace?
examples.note: 'En terrasse' = on the terrace. The terrace is very popular in France.

examples.original: Comme entrée, je voudrais la soupe à l'oignon.
examples.phonetic: /kɔm ɑ̃tʁe ʒə vudʁɛ la sup a lɔɲɔ̃/
examples.translation: For starter, I would like the onion soup.
examples.note: 'Comme entrée/plat/dessert' for each part of the meal.

examples.original: Je prends le menu à vingt euros.
examples.translation: I'll have the twenty-euro menu.
examples.note: 'Je prends' = I'll have. 'Le menu' = fixed-price menu (3 courses).

examples.original: Et comme boisson, une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
examples.phonetic: /e kɔm bwasɔ̃ yn kaʁaf do sil vu plɛ/
examples.translation: And to drink, a carafe of water, please.
examples.note: Tap water is free in France: 'une carafe d'eau' (carafe of water).

examples.original: Est-ce que c'est possible sans gluten?
examples.translation: Is it possible without gluten?
examples.note: 'Sans' = without. 'Sans gluten, sans lactose, sans noix' = without gluten, without lactose, without nuts.

examples.original: C'est délicieux! Mes compliments au chef.
examples.translation: It's delicious! My compliments to the chef.
examples.note: Expressing satisfaction. French people greatly value appreciating the food.

examples.original: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. On paie séparément.
examples.phonetic: /ladisjɔ̃ sil vu plɛ ɔ̃ pɛ sepaʁemɑ̃/
examples.translation: The bill, please. We pay separately.
examples.note: 'Séparément' = separately. In France it is normal to ask for separate bills.

title: Faire des achats / Basic Shopping
bridge: Shopping in France has its rituals. As in restaurants, you must always greet when entering any store: 'Bonjour!' is mandatory. To ask the price: 'C'est combien?' or 'Ça coûte combien?' are the most natural. One particularity: in France, fruits and vegetables at markets are weighed and the price is indicated per kilo. You should also know that 'un euro' is written with the symbol € and pronounced 'un euro', and cents are 'centimes'.
rule: Asking price: C'est combien? / Ça coûte combien? / Quel est le prix? Asking for something: Je voudrais + quantity + noun, Vous avez + noun?, Est-ce que vous avez...? Sizes and colors: Je cherche quelque chose en rouge, taille M. Payment methods: Je paie par carte / en espèces (cash) / avec mon téléphone. Useful expressions: C'est trop cher (it's too expensive), Vous faites les soldes? (Do you have sales?), Je peux l'essayer? (Can I try it on?).

concept_examples.translation: How much is this sweater?

concept_examples.text: Je voudrais deux kilos de tomates.
concept_examples.translation: I would like two kilos of tomatoes.

concept_examples.text: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte?
concept_examples.translation: Can I pay by card?
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɛs kə ʒə pø peje paʁ kaʁt/

concept_examples.text: Je cherche quelque chose en rouge, taille M.
concept_examples.translation: I'm looking for something in red, size M.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʒə ʃɛʁʃ kɛlkə ʃoz ɑ̃ ʁuʒ taj ɛm/

common_error.wrong: Combien coûte ce? / Combien ceci coûte?
common_error.correct: C'est combien, ça? / Ça coûte combien?
common_error.correct_alt: Quel est le prix de ceci?
common_error.explanation: 'C'est combien?' and 'Ça coûte combien?' are the most natural ways to ask the price in a shopping context. 'Quel est le prix?' is more formal. Avoid literal translations from Spanish.

examples.original: Excusez-moi, c'est combien ce sac?
examples.translation: Excuse me, how much is this bag?
examples.note: Always start with 'excusez-moi' to get attention in a store.

examples.original: Ça fait vingt-trois euros cinquante.
examples.translation: That's twenty-three euros fifty.
examples.note: 'Ça fait' = that's (total price). Cents: 23.50 = vingt-trois euros cinquante.

examples.original: Je peux payer en espèces?
examples.translation: Can I pay in cash?
examples.note: 'En espèces' = in cash. 'Par carte' = by card.

examples.original: Je cherche une robe pour une soirée.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə ʃɛʁʃ yn ʁɔb puʁ yn swaʁe/
examples.translation: I'm looking for a dress for a party.
examples.note: 'Chercher' = to look for. 'Pour une soirée' = for an evening/party.

examples.original: Est-ce que vous l'avez en bleu, taille 38?
examples.phonetic: /ɛs kə vu lave ɑ̃ blø taj tʁɑ̃t‿ɥit/
examples.translation: Do you have it in blue, size 38?
examples.note: Clothing sizes in France follow the European system. Size 38 ≈ S/M.

examples.original: Je peux l'essayer?
examples.translation: Can I try it on?
examples.note: 'Essayer' = to try (on). 'La cabine d'essayage' = the fitting room.

levels.label: Au marché et à l'épicerie
levels.translation: At the market and the grocery store

examples.original: Je voudrais un kilo de pommes et une baguette.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vudʁɛ œ̃ kilo də pɔm e yn baɡɛt/
examples.translation: I would like a kilo of apples and a baguette.
examples.note: The baguette is the most typical bread in France. It is bought fresh every day.

examples.original: Vous avez du fromage de chèvre?
examples.translation: Do you have goat cheese?
examples.note: 'Du fromage' = some cheese (partitive article). There are more than 1000 cheeses in France.

examples.original: C'est un peu trop cher pour moi. Vous pouvez faire un geste?
examples.phonetic: /sɛ tœ̃ pø tʁo ʃɛʁ puʁ mwa vu puve fɛʁ œ̃ ʒɛst/
examples.translation: It's a bit too expensive for me. Can you do something (a discount)?
examples.note: 'Faire un geste' = to give a discount/concession. At markets, negotiating is possible.

title: Demander et donner des indications / Asking for and giving directions
bridge: Asking for directions in French is a very common situation for travelers. The good news: many words are similar to Spanish. Some important differences: 'à gauche' (to the left), 'à droite' (to the right), 'tout droit' (straight ahead). The trap: 'la rue' (the street) is feminine, 'le boulevard' is masculine, 'l'avenue' is feminine. And for distances in France, the metric system is always used. A very useful expression: 'c'est à deux minutes à pied' (it's a two-minute walk).
rule: Asking for directions: Excusez-moi, où est...? / Pour aller à...? / Comment est-ce qu'on va à...? Direction vocabulary: à gauche (left), à droite (right), tout droit (straight ahead), tournez (turn), continuez (continue), prenez (take, for streets/transport), au carrefour (at the intersection), au feu (at the traffic light), au rond-point (at the roundabout), traversez (cross). Distances: c'est à X mètres/minutes à pied. Location: c'est en face de, à côté de, près de.

concept_examples.translation: Excuse me, how do I get to the Louvre?

concept_examples.text: Tournez à gauche et continuez tout droit.
concept_examples.translation: Turn left and continue straight ahead.
concept_examples.phonetic: /tuʁne a ɡoʃ e kɔ̃tinɥe tu dʁwa/

concept_examples.text: C'est à cinq minutes à pied.
concept_examples.translation: It's a five-minute walk.

concept_examples.text: Prenez la deuxième rue à droite.
concept_examples.translation: Take the second street on the right.

common_error.wrong: Vas à gauche et vas tout droit.
common_error.correct: Allez à gauche et continuez tout droit.
common_error.correct_alt: Va à gauche et continue tout droit. (informal)
common_error.explanation: To give directions, the imperative is used. 'Allez/Tournez/Continuez/Prenez' are 'vous' (formal) forms. 'Va/Tourne/Continue/Prends' are 'tu' (informal) forms. The imperative of 'aller' is irregular: allez (vous), va (tu).

examples.original: Excusez-moi, où se trouve la gare?
examples.phonetic: /ɛkskyze mwa u sə tʁuv la ɡaʁ/
examples.translation: Excuse me, where is the station?
examples.note: 'Où se trouve' = where is located. More formal than 'où est'.

examples.original: Pour aller au musée d'Orsay, s'il vous plaît?
examples.phonetic: /puʁ ale o myze dɔʁsɛ sil vu plɛ/
examples.translation: How do I get to the Musée d'Orsay, please?
examples.note: 'Pour aller à/au/aux' = to go to. Very natural for asking directions.

examples.original: C'est loin d'ici?
examples.translation: Is it far from here?
examples.note: 'Loin d'ici' = far from here. 'Près d'ici' = near here.

examples.original: Allez tout droit, puis tournez à droite.
examples.phonetic: /ale tu dʁwa pɥi tuʁne a dʁwat/
examples.translation: Go straight ahead, then turn right.
examples.note: 'Puis' = then, afterwards. Very useful connector for chaining directions.

examples.original: Prenez la première rue à gauche.
examples.translation: Take the first street on the left.
examples.note: 'La première/deuxième/troisième rue' = the first/second/third street.

examples.original: C'est juste en face de la mairie.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ ʒyst ɑ̃ fas də la mɛʁi/
examples.translation: It's right across from the town hall.
examples.note: 'Juste' here = just/right. 'La mairie' = the town hall. Typical reference in France.

examples.original: Continuez jusqu'au feu, puis traversez.
examples.translation: Continue to the traffic light, then cross.
examples.note: 'Jusqu'au' = until the. 'Au feu' = at the traffic light. 'Traverser' = to cross.

examples.original: Prenez le métro ligne 4 et descendez à Châtelet.
examples.phonetic: /pʁəne lə metʁo liɲ katʁ e desɑ̃de a ʃatlɛ/
examples.translation: Take metro line 4 and get off at Châtelet.
examples.note: 'Prendre le métro' = to take the metro. 'Descendre à' = to get off at.

examples.original: C'est à environ dix minutes en voiture.
examples.phonetic: /sɛ ta ɑ̃viʁɔ̃ dis minyt ɑ̃ vwatyʁ/
examples.translation: It's about a ten-minute drive.
examples.note: 'Environ' = approximately. 'En voiture/à pied/en vélo' = by car/on foot/by bike.

title: Parler de la famille / Talking about family
bridge: French family vocabulary has some interesting peculiarities. 'Parent' can mean both 'father' and 'relative' (in the plural 'les parents' = parents OR relatives, depending on context). 'Beau-père' can be father-in-law OR stepfather, just like in Spanish. A trap: in modern French, informal terms are widely used: 'maman/papa' (mom/dad), 'papi/mamie' (grandpa/grandma in an affectionate version).
rule: Immediate family: le père (father), la mère (mother), les parents (parents/relatives), le frère (brother), la sœur (sister), le fils (son), la fille (daughter), le mari (husband), la femme (wife/woman), le/la partenaire (partner). Extended family: le grand-père (grandfather), la grand-mère (grandmother), l'oncle (uncle), la tante (aunt), le cousin/la cousine (cousin), le neveu/la nièce (nephew/niece). In-laws: le beau-père (father-in-law/stepfather), la belle-mère (mother-in-law/stepmother).

concept_examples.text: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
concept_examples.translation: I have one brother and two sisters.
My parents live in Lyon.
My grandmother is eighty-two years old.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ma ɡʁɑ̃ mɛʁ a katʁ vɛ̃ dø zɑ̃/

concept_examples.translation: I am an only son.

common_error.explanation: 'La fille' = the daughter (also = the girl). 'Le fils' = the son (pronounced /fis/, the s is not silent). Do not confuse 'ma femme' (my wife) with 'ma fille' (my daughter). 'Femme' means both 'woman' and 'wife'.

examples.original: Voici ma famille: mon père, ma mère et ma sœur.
examples.phonetic: /vwasi ma famij mɔ̃ pɛʁ ma mɛʁ e ma sœʁ/
examples.translation: This is my family: my father, my mother, and my sister.
examples.note: 'Voici' = here is/here are. Used to introduce people and things.

examples.original: Mon mari s'appelle Antoine et nous avons deux enfants.
examples.phonetic: /mɔ̃ maʁi sapɛl ɑ̃twan e nuz‿avɔ̃ dø zɑ̃fɑ̃/
examples.translation: My husband is called Antoine and we have two children.
examples.note: 'Les enfants' = the children/the kids (both meanings).

examples.original: J'ai une petite sœur de douze ans.
examples.translation: I have a little sister who is twelve years old.
examples.note: 'Petite sœur' = younger sister. 'Grande sœur' = older sister.

examples.original: Mes grands-parents habitent à la campagne.
examples.phonetic: /me ɡʁɑ̃ paʁɑ̃ nabit a la kɑ̃paɲ/
examples.translation: My grandparents live in the countryside.
examples.note: 'Les grands-parents' = the grandparents (both). 'À la campagne' = in the countryside.

examples.original: J'ai beaucoup de cousins et cousines.
examples.translation: I have many male and female cousins.
examples.note: 'Cousin' (masc.) / 'cousine' (fem.). 'Beaucoup de' = many/a lot of.

examples.original: Mon oncle et ma tante ont trois enfants.
examples.phonetic: /mɔ̃ nɔ̃kl e ma tɑ̃t ɔ̃ tʁwa zɑ̃fɑ̃/
examples.translation: My uncle and my aunt have three children.
examples.note: 'Oncle' = uncle, 'tante' = aunt. Different from 'mononcle/ma tante' (colloquial).

levels.label: Décrire sa famille et ses relations

examples.original: Je suis proche de ma mère mais j'ai du mal avec mon père.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə sɥi pʁɔʃ də ma mɛʁ mɛ ʒe dy mal avɛk mɔ̃ pɛʁ/
examples.translation: I am close to my mother but I have a hard time with my father.
examples.note: 'Être proche de' = to be close to. 'Avoir du mal avec' = to have difficulty with.

examples.original: Mes parents sont divorcés, j'ai un beau-père.
examples.phonetic: /me paʁɑ̃ sɔ̃ divɔʁse ʒe œ̃ bopɛʁ/
examples.translation: My parents are divorced, I have a stepfather.
examples.note: 'Divorcé(e)' = divorced. 'Beau-père' = stepfather OR father-in-law depending on context.

examples.original: On se retrouve en famille tous les dimanches.
examples.phonetic: /ɔ̃ sə ʁətʁuv ɑ̃ famij tu le dimɑ̃ʃ/
examples.translation: We get together as a family every Sunday.
examples.note: 'Se retrouver en famille' = to get together as a family. A very French tradition.

title: Exprimer besoin et désir / Expressing need and desire
bridge: To express needs and desires in French there are several structures. The most important and polite is 'je voudrais' (conditional of vouloir = to want), equivalent to the Spanish 'quisiera'. 'J'ai besoin de' (I need) is literal: 'j'ai' (I have) + 'besoin' (need) + 'de'. A trap for Spanish speakers: you don't say 'je nécessite' as a calque of 'necesito'; the correct and natural form is 'j'ai besoin de'. 'Il me faut' (I need) is another very useful form.
rule: Expressing desire: Je voudrais + infinitive/noun (I would like...), J'aimerais + infinitive (I would like...), Je veux + infinitive (I want, more direct). Expressing need: J'ai besoin de + noun/infinitive, Il me faut + noun (I need), Il faut que + subjunctive (one must, impersonal). Expressing intention: J'ai l'intention de + infinitive (I intend to), Je vais + infinitive (near future). Maximum politeness: Pourriez-vous...? (Could you...?).

concept_examples.text: J'ai besoin d'aide, s'il vous plaît.
concept_examples.translation: I need help, please.
I would like to learn French.

concept_examples.text: Il me faut un stylo et du papier.
concept_examples.translation: I need a pen and some paper.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il mə fo œ̃ stilo e dy papje/

concept_examples.translation: I would like to visit Mont-Saint-Michel.

common_error.explanation: 'Nécessiter' exists in French but is very formal and technical (used mainly in written French). In everyday conversation, 'avoir besoin de' (to have need of) or 'il me faut' (I need) is always used to express need.

levels.label: Exprimer un désir: je voudrais, j'aimerais
levels.translation: Expressing a desire: je voudrais, j'aimerais

examples.original: Je voudrais une chambre pour deux nuits.
examples.phonetic: /ʒə vudʁɛ yn ʃɑ̃bʁ puʁ dø nɥi/
examples.translation: I would like a room for two nights.
examples.note: 'Je voudrais' = I would like. The most polite and used form to ask for something.

examples.original: J'aimerais parler avec le directeur.
examples.translation: I would like to speak with the director.
examples.note: 'J'aimerais' is the conditional of 'aimer', softer than 'je voudrais'.

examples.original: Je veux changer de travail.
examples.translation: I want to change jobs.
examples.note: 'Je veux' = I want. More direct/decided than 'je voudrais'. Appropriate among friends.

levels.label: Exprimer un besoin: j'ai besoin de, il me faut
levels.translation: Expressing a need: j'ai besoin de, il me faut

examples.original: J'ai besoin de dormir, je suis épuisé.
examples.translation: I need to sleep, I'm exhausted.
examples.note: 'J'ai besoin de + infinitive' = I need to + infinitive.

examples.original: Il me faut votre passeport, monsieur.
examples.translation: I need your passport, sir.
examples.note: 'Il me faut + noun' = I need. Impersonal and formal.

examples.original: Est-ce qu'il y a quelque chose que tu as besoin?
examples.phonetic: /ɛs kil ja kɛlkə ʃoz kə ty a bəzwɛ̃/
examples.translation: Is there something you need?
examples.note: 'Tu as besoin de quelque chose?' is more natural to ask if someone needs something.

levels.label: Exprimer une intention et demander poliment
levels.translation: Expressing an intention and asking politely

examples.original: J'ai l'intention de voyager en France l'été prochain.
examples.phonetic: /ʒe lɑ̃tɑ̃sjɔ̃ də vwajaʒe ɑ̃ fʁɑ̃s lete pʁɔʃɛ̃/
examples.translation: I intend to travel to France next summer.
examples.note: 'Avoir l'intention de + infinitive' = to intend to.

examples.original: Pourriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît?
examples.translation: Could you help me, please?
examples.note: 'Pourriez-vous' = could you? The maximum level of politeness in requests.

examples.original: Il faudrait que je parte maintenant.
examples.translation: I should leave now.
examples.note: 'Il faudrait que + subjunctive' = it would be necessary that. Expresses soft obligation.

title: Exprimer un besoin et un désir / Expressing need and desire
bridge: In Spanish, to express need and desire we use verbs like 'necesitar', 'querer', and the structure 'tener que'. In French, the equivalents are 'avoir besoin de', 'vouloir', and 'devoir'. A common mistake for Spanish speakers is saying 'je besoin' instead of 'j'ai besoin', since in Spanish the verb 'necesitar' is used directly. Also, 'vouloir' is an irregular verb with a specific pronunciation (the final 'l' is not pronounced). Pay attention to the agreement of the partitive article after 'besoin de'.
rule: To express need in French, use the structure 'avoir besoin de' + noun or infinitive. The verb 'avoir' is conjugated according to the subject. To express desire, use the verb 'vouloir' (to want), which is irregular in the present tense: je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent. Also use 'devoir' (must/have to) for necessity or obligation: je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils/elles doivent. Remember that with 'besoin de' an article (un, une, des, du, de la) or an infinitive is used. Examples: 'J'ai besoin d'eau', 'Tu as besoin de dormir', 'Elle veut un café'.

concept_examples.translation: I need help.
I want a croissant.
You have to study.
She needs rest.

common_error.explanation: The error comes from literally translating 'necesitar' as 'besoigner', which does not exist in modern French. The correct form is to use 'avoir besoin de'. Avoid saying 'je besoin'; always conjugate the verb 'avoir' before 'besoin'.

examples.original: J'ai besoin d'un stylo.
examples.translation: I need a pen.
examples.note: Use 'd'un' because 'stylo' is masculine singular.

examples.original: Nous avons besoin d'eau.
examples.translation: We need water.
examples.note: 'Eau' starts with a vowel, so 'd'eau' is used (contraction of 'de + eau').

examples.original: Ils ont besoin d'argent.
examples.translation: They need money.
examples.note: Remember that 'ils' is masculine plural; the pronunciation of 'ont' is /ɔ̃/.

examples.original: Je veux un café.
examples.translation: I want a coffee.
examples.note: 'Veux' is pronounced /vø/ without pronouncing the final 'x'.

examples.original: Tu veux une pomme ?
examples.translation: Do you want an apple?
examples.note: The rising intonation turns the sentence into a question.

examples.original: Nous voulons voyager.
examples.translation: We want to travel.
examples.note: After 'vouloir', another verb is used in the infinitive.

examples.original: Elles veulent un gâteau.
examples.translation: They want a cake.
examples.note: The ending 'ent' is not pronounced, but the form is 'veulent'.

examples.original: Je dois partir.
examples.translation: I must leave.
examples.note: Use 'devoir + infinitive' to express obligation.

examples.original: Tu dois ranger ta chambre.
examples.translation: You have to tidy your room.
examples.note: 'Ta chambre' is feminine singular, so 'ta'.

examples.original: Nous devons faire nos devoirs.
examples.translation: We must do our homework.
examples.note: The final 's' of 'nous' is pronounced as /z/ before a vowel.

examples.original: Vous devez acheter du pain.
examples.translation: You have to buy bread.
examples.note: 'Du pain' uses the partitive article because it is an indefinite quantity.
